newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli Arabs carry Syrian "message of peace".
newsitem.headline: Israeli Arabs carry Syrian "message of peace".

text.p: An Israeli Arab delegation returned from a rare trip to Damascus on Friday saying they carried a message of peace from Syrian President Hafez al-Assad.
But opposition politicians in the group said Syria saw little chance of reaching a peace accord with the present Israeli government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"The main message is that the Syrian leadership headed by President Assad wants real peace. He said clearly that 'With Bibi (Netanyahu), it will be hard for us to make peace'", member of parliament Saleh Tarif said on his return.
The 44 Israeli Arabs -- only the second such delegation to visit Damascus in 50 years -- spent a week in Syria at Assad's invitation.
They said the Syrian president was sending an olive branch to the Israeli public after more than a year of deadlock in peace talks between the two countries.

"I believe there is a true attempt by the Syrian leadership to change the policy to a more open policy toward public opinion in Israel and this visit is a most important visit," Tarif told Israel Radio at Tel Aviv airport.
Tarif, a Druze who is a reserve major in Israel's armed forces, said before the trip he would be the first Israeli army officer to shake hands with a Syrian president.
No Syrian-Israeli peace talks have occurred since the May 1996 election of Netanyahu, who rejects Syrian demands for the return of the Golan Heights that Israel captured in 1967.
Former Labour governments of Shimon Peres and Yitzhak Rabin had been willing to trade at least part of the strategic plateau for peace.
Last month Netanyahu backed, in a preliminary vote, a bill that would make it harder for parliament to cede the Golan.

"I believe the message was clear of President Assad, his foreign minister, of the Syrian people -- that they're ready to recognise Israel, to reach a peace treaty based on a full withdrawal for a full peace," said member of parliament Abdul-Wahab Darawshe.
"For whoever wants peace with Syria, here's a formula suitable for peace," he said.
But he said Netanyahu was ignoring the signals of "flexibility" from Damascus.
"The problem is here, in Israel. We have not a prime minister and a government that...are ready to welcome any message of peace from Syria," Darawshe said.
Tarif said in Damascus he was carrying with him a call from Labour party leader Ehud Barak to the Syrian leadership to coordinate peace efforts.
"President Assad himself said he can make peace with Ehud Barak and believes that with him he can continue from the very point that the talks ended with both Peres and the late Rabin," he said.
The group travelled via Egypt, the first Arab state to make peace with Israel, because there are no direct flights between Israel and Syria.
